41	1 Introduction
42	Scaling laws continue to reward larger model capacity [8, 26].
43	Frontier LLMs therefore increasingly use sparse Mixture-
44	of-Experts (MoE) modules that dynamically activate a few
45	experts to add parameters without proportionally increasing
46	computation [13, 17, 27, 33, 40, 51]. It is still challenging to
47	serve them efficiently, because instances must still store mas-
48	sive expert weights, while token-dependent routing makes
49	expert computation and communication vary across tokens.
50	Modern LLM serving systems typically use prefill-decode
51	disaggregation (PDD) to serve MoE LLMs to avoid interfer-
52	ence between the compute-intensive prefill phase and the
53	latency-sensitive decode phase [13, 23, 38, 39, 58]. For better
54	performance, PDD also needs to allocate resources accord-
55	ing to the P:D ratio that matches the resource demands of
56	two phases. However, existing instance-level PDD provisions
57	a complete model replica for each phase, so its allocation
58	granularity grows with the model. A reported DeepSeek-V3
59	deployment uses 32 GPUs for prefill and 320 GPUs for de-
60	code in one unit [ 13] to achieve this ratio. Small clusters
61	cannot realize this ratio, leading to resource waste. Large
62	clusters can achieve this ratio, but suffer from a larger failure
63	blast radius because a rank failure in hierarchical communi-
64	cation can stall the entire unit [15, 44]. They can also scale
65	only at the granularity of the large deployment unit when
66	traffic shifts. Duplicated expert weights also displace KV
67	cache. PDD therefore obtains isolation at the cost of memory
68	efficiency, elasticity, and fault containment.
69	Prefill-decode colocation solutions instead use Green Con-
70	text [36] to reserve SMs for each phase to achieve weight
71	deduplication and computation multiplexing [ 10, 22, 41],

74	nel, and reconfiguration is limited at the prefill layer level

79	changes in expert activation on each GPU [20, 21, 47]. Coarse

waits make per-kernel changes impractical. Existing systems
therefore repartition at the prefill layer boundary [10, 41].
As Figure 2 illustrates, a poor partition creates two fail-
ure modes. If prefill holds too many SMs when decode be-
comes ready, latency-sensitive decode waits behind a non-
preemptible prefill kernel. This head-of-line blocking can be
severe because a prefill kernel may run for tens to hundreds
of milliseconds while a decode kernel finishes in hundreds
of microseconds, a difference of orders of magnitude. If re-
sources remain reserved for decode when it has no ready
work, prefill cannot use them, and the GPU develops a re-
source bubble. Rank-varying EP load and different module
characteristics compound both problems.
Existing solutions also leave communication unisolated.
Prefill and decode dispatch and combine share the same
NICs and links, where a large prefill transfer can throttle a
small latency-sensitive decode transfer. Conventional two-
sided communication further requires matching two-sided
progress. Independent scheduling can leave some MoE ranks
serving prefill while others serve decode, so each phase waits
for receiver work on ranks occupied by the other, and the
system deadlocks. Finally, partitioning every GPU gives each
phase fewer local resources.
